title: Connectedness
objectives: Prove that intervals are connected, and derive the intermediate value theorem from it.

screens.title: Split it in two
screens.prose: On $X = \{a, b, c\}$ take $\tau = \{\varnothing, \{a\}, \{b, c\}, X\}$. We want two open sets that are disjoint, non-empty, and together make $X$.
screens.question: Tap two open sets that split $X$.

hints.text: Both must be non-empty, so leave out $\varnothing$.
$\{a\}$ and $\{b, c\}$ are disjoint and cover $X$.

feedback.correct: Right. This space falls into two open pieces.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find two disjoint non-empty open sets whose union is $X$.

byKey.e: $\varnothing$ is empty, so it does not count as a piece.

explain.text: $\{a\}$ and $\{b, c\}$ are open, disjoint, non-empty and cover $X$. Such a pair is a **separation**.

screens.title: No split at all
screens.prose: Now take $\tau = \{\varnothing, \{a\}, \{b\}, \{a, b\}, X\}$ on $\{a, b, c\}$.
screens.question: Which pair of open sets splits $X$?

options.text: No pair: the only open set holding $c$ is $X$

options.why: They are disjoint, but their union $\{a, b\}$ misses $c$.

options.text: $\{a, b\}$ and $X$

hints.text: One of the two sets must hold $c$.
Only $X$ holds $c$.
Then the other set would have to be empty.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Which open sets contain $c$?

explain.text: Whichever set holds $c$ must be $X$, leaving the other empty. So no separation exists: the space is **connected**.

screens.title: Three ways to say it
screens.prose: $X$ is **connected** when no separation exists. A set both open and closed is called **clopen**; a separation $U, V$ makes $U$ clopen, since $U^c = V$.

rows: no disjoint non-empty open $U, V$ with $U \cup V = X$
only $\varnothing$ and $X$ are open and closed

screens.question: Why does a non-constant continuous $f : X \to \{0, 1\}$ (discrete) give a separation?

options.text: $f^{-1}(0)$ and $f^{-1}(1)$ are open, disjoint, non-empty and cover $X$.
$f^{-1}(0)$ is closed, but it need not be open.
options.why: $\{0\}$ is open in the discrete space, so $f^{-1}(0)$ is open as well as closed.

options.text: $f$ is continuous, so $f(X)$ is closed.
options.why: Closedness of the image is not the point. The two preimages give the separation.

hints.text: $\{0\}$ and $\{1\}$ are open in the discrete space.
Pull both back.

feedback.correct: Right. The three conditions say the same thing.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Use preimages of the two points.

explain.text: Both singletons are open, so their preimages are open. They are disjoint and cover $X$, and non-empty because $f$ takes both values. So the three conditions are equivalent.

screens.title: Which sets fall apart?
screens.prose: Subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ with the subspace topology. A separation of $Y$ uses sets open in $Y$.
screens.question: Which sets are disconnected? Select all that apply.

options.text: $\mathbb{Q}$, split by $(-\infty, \sqrt2)$ and $(\sqrt2, \infty)$
$\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$, split into its two halves

options.why: Intervals are connected; the next screen proves it.

hints.text: Look for a missing point to cut at.

$\sqrt2 
otin \mathbb{Q}$, $0 
otin \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$, $1 
otin (0, 1) \cup (1, 2)$.

feedback.correct: Right. Each has a gap to cut at.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find a point outside the set that it surrounds.

explain.text: Cutting at a missing point gives two open halves. $\mathbb{Q}$ misses $\sqrt2$, so even a dense set can be disconnected. $[0, 1]$ has no gap.

screens.title: Intervals are connected
screens.prose: Suppose $[a, b] = U \cup V$ with $U, V$ disjoint, non-empty and open in $[a, b]$, and $a \in U$. We reach a contradiction. One line is flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: Let $c = \sup\{x \in [a, b] : [a, x] \subseteq U\}$, which exists by completeness of $\mathbb{R}$.
If $c \in V$, a ball round $c$ lies in the open $V$. Yet points just left of $c$ are in $U$. Contradiction.
So $c \in U$. If $c < b$, a ball round $c$ lies in $U$, so $[a, c + \delta] \subseteq U$, beyond the supremum. Contradiction.
So $c = b \in U$ and $[a, b] \subseteq U$, leaving $V$ empty. Contradiction: $[a, b]$ is connected. $\blacksquare$
Let $c$ be the largest point of $U$.
lines.why: An open set need not have a largest point: $[0, 0.5)$ is open in $[0, 1]$ and has none.

hints.text: Use a supremum, since a maximum may not exist.
Show $c$ is in neither $V$ nor $U \cap [a, b)$, so $c = b$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Define $c$ by a supremum, then rule out each case.

byKey.d1: You took a largest point of $U$. Open sets need not have one; the supremum always exists.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: The supremum $c$ cannot lie in $V$, and cannot be a point of $U$ below $b$. So $c = b$ and $V$ is empty. Completeness was essential: in $\mathbb{Q}$ the same set is disconnected.

screens.title: Images of connected spaces
screens.prose: Let $f : X \to Y$ be continuous and $X$ connected. We show $f(X)$ is connected.
screens.question: Put the proof in order.

lines.text: Suppose $U, V$ separate $f(X)$: open in $f(X)$, disjoint, non-empty, with union $f(X)$.
Then $f^{-1}(U)$ and $f^{-1}(V)$ are open in $X$, by continuity.
They are disjoint, non-empty and cover $X$, because $U$ and $V$ are and lie inside $f(X)$.
That separates $X$, a contradiction. So $f(X)$ is connected. $\blacksquare$

hints.text: Pull a separation back.
Preimages of open sets are open (l4).

feedback.correct: Right. Preimages carry the separation back.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Start from a separation of $f(X)$.

explain.text: A separation of $f(X)$ pulls back to two disjoint non-empty open sets covering $X$. Since $X$ has no separation, neither does $f(X)$.

screens.title: Connected subsets of the line
screens.prose: Call $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ an **interval** when $x < y < z$ with $x, z \in I$ forces $y \in I$.
screens.question: Why is a connected $C \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ an interval?

options.text: If $x, z \in C$ but $y \notin C$ between them, then $(-\infty, y)$ and $(y, \infty)$ separate $C$.
A connected set is closed, so it is a closed interval.
A connected set is bounded, so it lies in some $[a, b]$.

hints.text: Suppose a point $y$ is missing between two points of $C$.
Cut at the missing $y$.
Both halves meet $C$, at $x$ and at $z$.

feedback.correct: Right. A gap gives a separation.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Cut at a missing point between two points of $C$.

explain.text: A missing $y$ between $x$ and $z$ splits $C$ by the open rays on either side, each meeting $C$. Every interval is a union of closed intervals through one point, so it is connected (homework 2 proves that step). So the connected subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ are exactly the intervals.

screens.title: The intermediate value theorem again
screens.prose: `analysis` l16 proved this by a supremum. Now it follows in four lines from connectedness. Let $f : [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous, and $y$ lie strictly between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$.
screens.question: Put the proof that $f(c) = y$ for some $c$ in order.

lines.text: Then $f^{-1}((-\infty, y))$ and $f^{-1}((y, \infty))$ are open, disjoint and cover $[a, b]$.
They are non-empty: one holds $a$ and the other $b$, since $y$ is strictly between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$.
That separates $[a, b]$, which is connected. So $f(c) = y$ for some $c \in [a, b]$. $\blacksquare$

hints.text: If $y$ is missed, cut the target line at $y$.
Pull the two rays back to $[a, b]$.

feedback.correct: Right. The theorem is connectedness in disguise.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Assume $y$ is missed, then pull back the two rays.

explain.text: If $y$ is missed, the two rays pull back to a separation of $[a, b]$. That contradicts the interval proof, so $y$ is hit.

screens.title: Two pieces, still connected
screens.prose: A learner writes $[0, 2] = [0, 1) \cup [1, 2]$: two disjoint non-empty pieces. "So $[0, 2]$ is disconnected."
screens.question: What is wrong with the argument?

options.text: $[1, 2]$ is not open in $[0, 2]$: every interval round 1 meets $[0, 1)$. A separation needs open pieces.
Nothing: any split into disjoint pieces disconnects a set.
options.why: You split into any pieces. Every set with two points splits so; the pieces of a separation must be open.

options.text: The pieces share the point 1.
options.why: They do not: 1 is in $[1, 2]$ only. The failure is openness.

hints.text: Are both pieces open in $[0, 2]$?
Look at the point 1.
Every ball round 1 holds points of $[0, 1)$.

feedback.correct: Right. Disjoint pieces are not enough.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Test whether each piece is open in $[0, 2]$.

byKey.fine: You took any disjoint split as a separation. Both pieces must be open, and $[1, 2]$ is not open at 1.

explain.text: Round 1 every relative ball meets $[0, 1)$, so $[1, 2]$ is not open in $[0, 2]$. Equivalently $[0, 1)$ is not closed there. A separation needs two open pieces, and $[0, 2]$ has none.

screens.title: Connected without a path
screens.prose: The **topologist's sine curve** is the graph of $\sin(\tfrac1x)$ for $0 < x \le 1$, together with the segment $\{0\} \times [-1, 1]$. A set is **path-connected** when a continuous path joins any two of its points.
screens.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: It is connected, but no path joins 0 to $(1, \sin 1)$.
It is disconnected: the curve never reaches the segment.
options.why: The curve's closure contains the whole segment, so no open split separates them.

options.text: It is path-connected, since it is connected.
options.why: Connected does not imply path-connected. A path would have to settle as $x \to 0$, and $\sin(\tfrac1x)$ never does.

hints.text: Every point of the segment is a limit of curve points.
A path from the curve to 0 would need $\sin(\tfrac1x)$ to converge.

feedback.correct: Right. An edge case the course does not pursue.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Separate the questions: connected, and path-connected.

explain.text: The curve is connected, as a continuous image of $(0, 1]$, and the segment lies in its closure. A closure of a connected set is connected. But no path reaches the segment, since $\sin(\tfrac1x)$ keeps oscillating; path-connectedness is not otherwise taught here.

screens.title: Components by machine
screens.prose: Write `is_connected(X, tau)`: no proper non-empty open set has an open complement. Then `components(X, tau)` returns the components as sorted strings, such as `['a', 'bc']`. On a finite space the component of $x$ is the intersection of the clopen sets holding $x$. Checking cases is evidence, not proof.
screens.question: Complete both functions.

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests, compared exactly. They cover connected and two-component spaces on three points, the discrete and indiscrete spaces, and two four-point spaces. The first Check starts Python in the browser, about 4 s once.

hints.text: A clopen set is an open set whose complement is also in `tau`.
Intersect the clopen sets that hold each point.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the clopen sets first.

explain.text: The clopen sets cut a finite space into its components. $\{\varnothing, \{a\}, \{b, c\}, X\}$ has components $\{a\}$ and $\{b, c\}$. Of the 29 topologies on three points, 19 are connected.

screens.title: Every return in between
screens.prose: Three assets have expected returns 4%, 6% and 9%. Long-only portfolios form the triangle of l6, which is connected. Expected return is continuous, so the attainable returns form an interval: $[4\%, 9\%]$. So 7% is attainable.
screens.question: Mix only the 4% and 9% assets. What weight on the 9% asset gives 7%?

feedback.generic: Not quite. The return rises linearly from 4% to 9% as $w$ goes from 0 to 1.

byKey.swap: 0.4 is the weight on the 4% asset. The 9% asset carries 0.6.
byKey.ratio: You divided 7 by 9. The return runs from 4%, not from 0.

explain.text: $0.4 \times 4\% + 0.6 \times 9\% = 7\%$, and $(0, \tfrac23, \tfrac13)$ works too. A parameter set with two components traps a local optimiser in the component it starts in.

ideas: A space is connected when no two disjoint non-empty open sets cover it. Equivalently only $\varnothing$ and $X$ are clopen, or every continuous map to $\{0, 1\}$ is constant.
$[a, b]$ is connected, by a supremum and completeness. Continuous images of connected spaces are connected, and the connected subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ are the intervals.
These give the intermediate value theorem in four lines. Disjoint pieces are not enough: $[0, 2] = [0, 1) \cup [1, 2]$ is connected.

formula.name: Separation
formula.tex: X = U \cup V, \ U \cap V = \varnothing, \ U, V \ne \varnothing \text{ open}
formula.note: Connected means no such pair exists.

summary.trap: Splitting into disjoint pieces is not a separation unless both pieces are open: $[1, 2]$ is not open in $[0, 2]$.

quiz.prose: There are 4 topologies on $\{a, b\}$: indiscrete, two Sierpiński spaces and discrete.
quiz.question: How many of them are connected?

feedback.correct: Right. Only the discrete space splits.
feedback.generic: Not quite. A separation needs $\{a\}$ and $\{b\}$ both open.

byKey.one: The Sierpiński spaces are connected too: each has only one open singleton.
byKey.all: The discrete space splits into $\{a\}$ and $\{b\}$.

explain.text: A separation of $\{a, b\}$ needs both singletons open, which happens only in the discrete topology. So 3 of 4 are connected; on three points 19 of 29 are.

options.why: The image is connected, so it is an interval holding both values and everything between.

options.text: Exactly $[-2, 5]$ and nothing else
options.why: It must contain $[-2, 5]$, but $f$ may overshoot, for example up to 6.

feedback.correct: Right. The image is an interval holding $-2$ and 5.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The image of a connected set is an interval.

explain.text: $[0, 1]$ is connected, so $f([0, 1])$ is a connected subset of $\mathbb{R}$: an interval. It holds $-2$ and 5, so it contains $[-2, 5]$.

quiz.prose: Remove one point from the circle, and one point from the interval $(0, 1)$.
quiz.question: What does this show?

options.text: The circle is not homeomorphic to $(0, 1)$: it stays connected, while $(0, 1)$ splits.
They are homeomorphic, since both stay in one dimension.
options.why: Dimension alone does not decide it. Removing a point is the test, and it gives different results.

options.text: Both become disconnected, so it shows nothing.
options.why: A circle minus a point is an open arc, which is connected.

feedback.correct: Right. Connectedness after removing a point tells them apart.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Remove a point from each and test connectedness.

explain.text: A circle minus a point is an arc, homeomorphic to $(0, 1)$, so it is connected. $(0, 1)$ minus a point is disconnected. A homeomorphism would match these, so none exists.
